distinctiveFeatures: English studies meaning made through communication in English and related languages, across language, literature and creative writing, and is often studied jointly or with neighbouring subjects such as film, media, cultural or translation studies

Its distinctive emphasis is discourse and meaning, aesthetics and rhetoric: close and critical reading in context, analysis of written and spoken texts and reflection on reading, writing and interpretation
It joins critical and creative response, so producing new creative work sits beside interpretation and analysis
It values dialogue, debate and difference, and engages with diverse perspectives and with the discipline's own colonial, patriarchal and elitist history
It builds four core capacities named throughout: communication, collaboration, creativity and critical thinking
Teaching leans on small groups, independent and collaborative study, flipped lectures, use of libraries, archives and corpora and a capstone project
Assessment is deliberately diverse, from essays and examinations to digital objects, performance and portfolios

standards.rungBases: 4.1: the statement sets the minimum threshold standards a student will have shown at the award of honours; 4.2: most students perform well above it, judged with Annex D. The standards are one table with three columns, each headed by a rung definition (threshold: the minimum that should be reached; typical: the main cluster; excellent: a defining paragraph, recorded as 4.2.ex1) and the lead-in 'are able to'. Rows: generic skills (communication, affective language, digital, collaboration, creativity, critical thinking, evidence); subject knowledge (close reading, interpretation, then a paragraph spanning all three columns, recorded as 4.2.sk1 to sk3 with rung none); embedded understanding of EDI, access, sustainability and entrepreneurship; creative writing, with its own lead-in. Cells hold several bullets each, so the columns hold different numbers of items.

subjectSpecific.text: By the end of your English degree, you can read texts closely and critically, aware of their form and of their historical and linguistic setting.
By the end of your English degree, you can understand how language can be creative, and the aesthetic qualities of literary and other cultural works.
By the end of your English degree, you can analyse spoken and written texts and discourse, and respond to how language moves and persuades, using suitable methods and terms.
By the end of your English degree, you can think critically about what happens when you read, write and interpret.
By the end of your English degree, you can build your own imaginative and convincing readings of literary, critical, linguistic or creative material, perhaps by writing new creative work of your own.
By the end of your English degree, you can explain critically how demanding texts and ideas work and how they relate to each other over time.
Depending on the parts of English you study, you will know about what language gives you to express things.
Depending on the parts of English you study, you will know about literature or language across different periods and the main genres of prose, poetry and drama.
Depending on the parts of English you study, you will know about how wide the range of literature written in English is.
Depending on the parts of English you study, you will know about the varieties of English used in different regions and around the world.
Depending on the parts of English you study, you will know about the history and structure of English, its levels of analysis and how it works in discourse.
Depending on the parts of English you study, you will know about how culture, language, technology and money shape how, where and by whom texts are made and read.
Depending on the parts of English you study, you will know about the part readers and audiences play in shaping texts.
Depending on the parts of English you study, you will know about how different genres and media relate to each other.
Depending on the parts of English you study, you will know about the concepts and vocabulary of criticism, theory, linguistics and stylistics.

transferable.text: By the end of your English degree, you can communicate clearly, accurately and effectively, whether speaking, writing or through other means.

statements.appliesTo: graduates who have reached the excellent standard
statements.about: what defines the excellent standard
statements.paraphrase: Graduates at the excellent standard show the same capabilities at a higher level, with wide independent reading, original thought and expression and deep understanding; their work brings broad knowledge to bear subtly and effectively, with outstanding critical insight, analytical rigour and creativity.

forBeneficiary.text: If you reach the excellent level, you show the same skills at a higher level: you read widely on your own, think and write originally, understand deeply and use broad knowledge with subtlety, insight, rigour and creativity.

statements.appliesTo: graduates in English, by the elements of their degree
statements.about: subject knowledge for language elements
statements.paraphrase: Subject knowledge will differ with the parts of the degree and grow in range and depth across the three standards; for language it may cover analysing spoken, written and multimodal communication, the history, spread and varieties of English, its sub-disciplines and methods; students will understand and use the field's concepts and terms and apply scholarly bibliographic skills.

forPractitioner.text: For the language parts of an English degree, plan knowledge of English in use and in history, its varieties and sub-disciplines and its methods of analysis, and make sure students use the field's concepts and terms and its referencing skills.

forBeneficiary.text: If your degree includes English language, you will know how spoken, written and multimodal communication works, how English developed and varies and the main methods for studying it; and you will use the subject's concepts, terms and referencing skills.

statements.appliesTo: graduates in English, by the elements of their degree
